claim: Cell cycle control networks in yeasts and animals are highly similar in both physiological function and network structure.
source: The networks regulating cell division in yeasts and animals are highly similar in both physiological function and network structure (Figure 1) (Cross et al., 2011; Doonan and Kitsios, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cross et al., 2011 and Doonan and Kitsios, 2009

claim: Cell cycle controls proliferation in response to a variety of internal and external signals during the G1 phase, between cell division and DNA replication.
source: For example, the cell cycle controls proliferation in response to a variety of internal and external signals during the G1 phase, between cell division and DNA replication.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about cell cycle regulation

claim: Input signals, including cell growth, are integrated into a gradual increase in cyclin dependent kinase (Cdk) activity, which triggers a feedback loop at the basis of the all-or-none irreversible decision to proliferate.
source: These input signals, including cell growth, are integrated into a gradual increase in cyclin dependent kinase (Cdk) activity, which triggers a feedback loop at the basis of the all-or-none irreversible decision to proliferate (Bertoli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bertoli et al., 2013

claim: In animal cells, Cyclin D, in complex with either Cdk4 or Cdk6, initiates cell cycle entry by phosphorylating the retinoblastoma protein, pRb.
source: In animal cells, Cyclin D, in complex with either Cdk4 or Cdk6, initiates cell cycle entry by phosphorylating the retinoblastoma protein, pRb.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of animal cell cycle regulation

claim: Phosphorylation of pRb begins the inactivation of pRb and the concomitant activation of the E2F transcription factors that induce transcription of downstream cyclins E and A, which complete the inhibition of pRb thereby forming a positive feedback loop.
source: This begins the inactivation of pRb and the concomitant activation of the E2F transcription factors that induce transcription of downstream cyclins E and A, which complete the inhibition of pRb thereby forming a positive feedback loop (Bertoli et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bertoli et al., 2013

claim: In budding yeast, the G1 cyclin Cln3-Cdk1 complex initiates the transition by phosphorylating and partially inactivating Whi5, an inhibitor of the SBF transcription factor.
source: Similarly, in budding yeast, the G1 cyclin Cln3-Cdk1 complex initiates the transition by phosphorylating and partially inactivating Whi5, an inhibitor of the SBF transcription factor (Costanzo et al., 2004; de Bruin et al., 2004; Nasmyth and Dirick, 1991; Ogas et al., 1991; Sidorova and Breeden, 1993).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: SBF-dependent transcription of the downstream G1 cyclins CLN1 and CLN2 also inactivate Whi5 to complete a positive feedback loop.
source: This allows for SBF-dependent transcription of the downstream G1 cyclins CLN1 and CLN2, which also inactivate Whi5 to complete a positive feedback loop (Skotheim et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Skotheim et al., 2008

claim: The biochemical function of G1 regulators and their specific targets are highly conserved between animals and yeast.
source: Thus, both the biochemical function of G1 regulators and their specific targets are highly conserved (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by comparison of regulatory mechanisms and reference to Figure 1

claim: In yeast, a single cyclin-dependent kinase, Cdk1, binds distinct cyclin partners to perform all the functions of three non-orthologous animal Cdks (Cdk2, 4 and 6) during cell cycle entry.
source: In yeast, a single cyclin-dependent kinase, Cdk1, binds distinct cyclin partners to perform all the functions of three non-orthologous animal Cdks (Cdk2, 4 and 6) during cell cycle entry (Liu and Kipreos, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu and Kipreos, 2000

claim: No member of the transcription factor complex SBF-Whi5 exhibits amino acid sequence identity or structural similarity to any member of the E2F-pRb complex.
source: Furthermore, no member of the transcription factor complex SBF-Whi5 exhibits amino acid sequence identity or structural similarity to any member of the E2F-pRb complex (Cross et al., 2011; Hasan et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Cdk inhibitors such as Sic1 and p27 play analogous roles in yeast and mammals despite a total lack of sequence identity.
source: Finally, Cdk inhibitors such as Sic1 and p27 play analogous roles in yeast and mammals despite a total lack of sequence identity (Cross et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cross et al., 2011

claim: The similar network topology in budding yeast and animals suggests that this feature is more conserved than the constituent regulatory proteins.
source: Although identification of network topology is restricted to a few model organisms and is not as broad as sequence analysis, the similar network topology in budding yeast and animals suggests that this feature is more conserved than the constituent regulatory proteins (Cross et al., 2011; Doonan and Kitsios, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cross et al., 2011 and Doonan and Kitsios, 2009

claim: The shared presence of E2F-pRb within plants (Archaeaplastida) and animal (Metazoa) lineages suggests that this regulatory complex was present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor.
source: The shared presence of E2F-pRb within plants (Archaeaplastida) and animal (Metazoa) lineages would suggest that this regulatory complex, rather than the fungal SBF-Whi5 complex, was present in the last eukaryotic common ancestor (Cao et al., 2010; Doonan and Kitsios, 2009; Fang et al., 2006; Harashima et al., 2013; Hallmann, 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations and phylogenetic inference

claim: Fungi and animals are more closely related to one another than either is to plants.
source: The sequence divergence between G1 regulators is surprising because fungi and animals are more closely related to one another than either is to plants.
evidence: Supported by established phylogenetic knowledge

claim: The study examined a greater number of genomes covering most of eukaryotic diversity, including Excavata, Haptophyta, Cryptophyta, SAR (Stramenopiles, Alveolata, Rhizaria), Archaeplastida (plants), Amoebozoa, Apusozoa and the Opisthokonta (animals and fungi).
source: We examined a greater number of genomes covering most of eukaryotic diversity, including Excavata, Haptophyta, Cryptophyta, SAR (Stramenopiles, Alveolata, Rhizaria), Archaeplastida (plants), Amoebozoa, Apusozoa and the Opisthokonta (animals and fungi).
evidence: Describes the scope of the study's data collection

claim: LECA likely had complex cell cycle regulation involving at least one Cdk, multiple cyclin families, activating and inhibitory E2F transcription factors, and pRb-family pocket proteins.
source: Our results indicate that LECA likely had complex cell cycle regulation involving at least one Cdk, multiple cyclin families, activating and inhibitory E2F transcription factors, and pRb-family pocket proteins.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis across eukaryotic genomes

claim: The emergence of SBF-Whi5 is abrupt and distinguishes fungi from all other eukaryotes.
source: Identifying the LECA repertoire helps establish that the emergence of SBF-Whi5 is abrupt and distinguishes fungi from all other eukaryotes.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic distribution analysis

claim: Basal fungi can have both ancestral E2F-pRb and fungal SBF-Whi5 components.
source: We show that basal fungi can have both ancestral E2F-pRb and fungal SBF-Whi5 components.
evidence: Supported by genomic survey data

claim: SBF shows homology to KilA-N, a poorly characterized domain present in prokaryotic and eukaryotic DNA viruses.
source: Our data confirm that SBF shows homology to KilA-N, a poorly characterized domain present in prokaryotic and eukaryotic DNA viruses.
evidence: Supported by sequence homology analysis

claim: SBF is not derived from E2F (its functional analog) and likely emerged through horizontal gene transfer in the fungal ancestor.
source: Thus, SBF is not derived from E2F (its functional analog) and likely emerged through horizontal gene transfer in the fungal ancestor.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis and homology data

claim: SBF can regulate promoters with E2F binding sites in budding yeast.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we show that SBF can regulate promoters with E2F binding sites in budding yeast.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: A virally-derived SBF may have initially hijacked cell cycle control by activating transcription via the cis-regulatory elements targeted by the ancestral cell cycle regulator E2F, much like extant viral oncogenes.
source: We hypothesize that a virally-derived SBF may have initially hijacked cell cycle control by activating transcription via the cis-regulatory elements targeted by the ancestral cell cycle regulator E2F, much like extant viral oncogenes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from multiple lines of evidence

claim: All sequenced eukaryotic lineages have lost entire gene families that were present in LECA.
source: Indeed, all sequenced eukaryotic lineages have lost entire gene families that were present in LECA (Fritz-Laylin et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fritz-Laylin et al., 2010

claim: The prevailing view of the cell cycle in LECA is that it was based on a simple oscillator constructed with relatively few components.
source: In contrast to the growing consensus that LECA had an extensive repertoire of proteins, the prevailing view of the cell cycle in LECA is that it was based on a simple oscillator constructed with relatively few components (Coudreuse and Nurse, 2010; Nasmyth, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Coudreuse and Nurse, 2010 and Nasmyth, 1995

claim: According to the 'simple' LECA cell cycle model, an ancestral oscillation in Cyclin B-Cdk1 activity drove periodic DNA replication and DNA segregation.
source: According to the 'simple' LECA cell cycle model, an ancestral oscillation in Cyclin B-Cdk1 activity drove periodic DNA replication and DNA segregation, while other aspects of cell cycle regulation, such as G1 control, may have subsequently evolved in specific lineages.
evidence: Describes a prevailing model in the field

claim: Cdk activity of a single Cyclin B is sufficient to drive embryonic cell cycles in frogs.
source: The model was motivated by the fact that Cdk activity of a single Cyclin B is sufficient to drive embryonic cell cycles in frogs (Murray and Kirschner, 1989) and fission yeast (Stern and Nurse, 1996), and that many yeast G1 regulators have no eukaryotic orthologs (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Murray and Kirschner, 1989

claim: Cdk activity of a single Cyclin B is sufficient to drive cell cycles in fission yeast.
source: The model was motivated by the fact that Cdk activity of a single Cyclin B is sufficient to drive embryonic cell cycles in frogs (Murray and Kirschner, 1989) and fission yeast (Stern and Nurse, 1996), and that many yeast G1 regulators have no eukaryotic orthologs (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stern and Nurse, 1996

claim: Neither of the fungal regulators (SBF and Whi5) were found outside of Fungi.
source: While we did not find either of the fungal regulators (SBF and Whi5) outside of Fungi, we did find animal-like cell cycle regulators in Archaeplastida, Amoebozoa, SAR, Haptophyta, Cryptophyta, Excavata and Metazoa (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by genomic survey data presented in Figure 2

claim: Animal-like cell cycle regulators are found in Archaeplastida, Amoebozoa, SAR, Haptophyta, Cryptophyta, Excavata and Metazoa.
source: While we did not find either of the fungal regulators (SBF and Whi5) outside of Fungi, we did find animal-like cell cycle regulators in Archaeplastida, Amoebozoa, SAR, Haptophyta, Cryptophyta, Excavata and Metazoa (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by genomic survey data presented in Figure 2

claim: The cyclin sub-families (A, B, D, and E) known to regulate the cell cycle in metazoans are found across the major branches of eukaryotes.
source: For example, the cyclin sub-families (A, B, D, and E) known to regulate the cell cycle in metazoans (for cyclin phylogeny see Figure 2—figure supplement 2) are found across the major branches of eukaryotes.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: Examples of all three sub-families of E2F transcription factors (E2F1-6, DP, E2F7/8) and the pRb family of pocket proteins were found across eukaryotes.
source: We also found examples of all three sub-families of E2F transcription factors (E2F1-6, DP, E2F7/8) and the pRb family of pocket proteins (for E2F/DP and pRb phylogeny see Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in supplementary figures

claim: Nearly all species contain the APC specificity subunits Cdc20 and Cdh1/Fzr1, which regulate exit from mitosis and maintain low Cdk activity in G1.
source: Nearly all species contain the APC specificity subunits Cdc20 and Cdh1/Fzr1, which regulate exit from mitosis and maintain low Cdk activity in G1 (for Cdc20-family APC phylogeny see Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by genomic survey data and phylogenetic analysis

claim: The phylogenetic analyses tend to place the fungal regulators as sister groups to the metazoan regulators, as would be expected from the known eukaryotic species tree.
source: More broadly, our phylogenetic analyses tend to place the fungal regulators as sister groups to the metazoan regulators, as would be expected from the known eukaryotic species tree.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis results

claim: Many fungal and metazoan regulators were vertically inherited from an opisthokont ancestor rather than loss of these regulators in fungi followed by secondary acquisition through horizontal gene transfer.
source: These phylogenies are in agreement with the hypothesis that many fungal and metazoan regulators were vertically inherited from an opisthokont ancestor rather than loss of these regulators in fungi followed by secondary acquisition through horizontal gene transfer.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis and inference

claim: SBF is an important member of a larger family of winged helix-turn-helix transcription factors that includes Xbp1, Bqt4, and the APSES family (Acm1, Phd1, Sok2, Egf1, StuA).
source: SBF is an important member of a larger family of winged helix-turn-helix transcription factors that includes Xbp1, Bqt4, and the APSES family (Acm1, Phd1, Sok2, Egf1, StuA); see Materials and methods and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for a complete list of homologs in each fungal genome.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and classification

claim: The emergence of the new fungal regulators SBF and Whi5 is abrupt and occurs near the split of basal fungi from metazoans.
source: The emergence of the new fungal regulators SBF, which includes the large APSES family, and Whi5 is abrupt and occurs near the split of basal fungi from metazoans (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic distribution data shown in Figure 3

claim: The new regulators (SBF and Whi5) and ancestral regulators (E2F and Rb) co-exist broadly across basal fungi and the lineages formerly known as 'zygomycetes'.
source: Interestingly, the new regulators (SBF and Whi5) and ancestral regulators (E2F and Rb) co-exist broadly across basal fungi and the lineages formerly known as 'zygomycetes' (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by genomic survey data shown in Figure 3

claim: Zoosporic, basal fungi such as Chytrids (e.g., Spizellomyces punctatus) can have both fungal and animal cell cycle regulators, which likely represents the ancestral fungal hybrid network.
source: Zoosporic, basal fungi such as Chytrids (e.g., Spizellomyces punctatus) can have both fungal and animal cell cycle regulators, which likely represents the ancestral fungal hybrid network.
evidence: Supported by genomic data and phylogenetic inference

claim: SBF-Whi5 in budding yeast plays a similar role to E2F-pRb in animals.
source: SBF-Whi5 in budding yeast plays a similar role to E2F-pRb in animals, which suggests that these pathways were functionally redundant in an ancestral hybrid network.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of cell cycle regulation

claim: The redundancy of SBF-Whi5 and E2F-pRb pathways would lead to the evolutionary instability of the hybrid network.
source: This redundancy would lead to the evolutionary instability of the hybrid network and could explain why different constellations of components are present in the extant zygomycetes and basal fungi (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on inference from evolutionary theory and observed data

claim: The zygomycetes have lost pRb while retaining E2F, which was then abruptly lost in the transition to Dikarya.
source: For example, the zygomycetes have lost pRb while retaining E2F, which was then abruptly lost in the transition to Dikarya.
evidence: Supported by genomic survey data

claim: With the possible exception of Microsporidia, all fungi have retained SBF and never completely reverted back to the original ancestral state.
source: However, with the possible exception of Microsporidia, all fungi have retained SBF and never completely reverted back to the original ancestral state.
evidence: Supported by genomic survey data

claim: The E2F_TDP.hmm profile is specific to E2F/DP and the KilA-N.hmm profile is specific to SBF+APSES.
source: Our controls (H. sapiens genome, Figure 4A and S. cerevisiae genome, Figure 4B) demonstrate that E2F_TDP.hmm is specific to E2F/DP and that KilA-N.hmm is specific to SBF+APSES.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Genomes with hybrid network (S. punctatus and other basal fungi with both transcription factors) have both E2F/DP and SBF+APSES.
source: We show that genomes with hybrid network (S. punctatus, Figure 4C, and other basal fungi with both transcription factors, Figure 4D) have both E2F/DP and SBF+APSES.
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: E2F_TDP.hmm never hits an SBF+APSES transcription factor and KilA-N.hmm never hits an E2F transcription factor.
source: E2F_TDP.hmm never hits an SBF+APSES transcription factor and KilA-N.hmm never hits an E2F transcription factor (i.e. there are no scores on the diagonal of the panels in Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: SBF and other KilA-N domains have no more sequence identity to E2F than non-homologous proteins.
source: These data suggest that SBF and other KilA-N domains have no more sequence identity to E2F than non-homologous proteins.
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis data

claim: Non-fungal genomes only hit E2F/DP with the notable exception of Trichomonas vaginalis, the only non-fungal genome with E2F/DP and KilA-N homologs.
source: We find that non-fungal genomes only hit E2F/DP (Figure 4E) with the notable exception of Trichomonas vaginalis, the only non-fungal genome with E2F/DP and KilA-N homologs (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: The DNA-binding domains of SBF/MBF and E2F/DP are both structurally classified as members of the winged-helix-turn-helix (wHTH) family.
source: The DNA-binding domains of SBF/MBF (Taylor et al., 1997; Xu et al., 1997) and E2F/DP (Zheng et al., 1999) are structurally classified as members of the winged-helix-turn-helix (wHTH) family, which is found in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes (Aravind and Koonin, 1999; Aravind et al., 2005; Gajiwala and Burley, 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to structural studies

claim: The DNA-binding domains of E2F/DP and SBF/MBF show important differences in overall structure and mode of protein-DNA complex formation that lead to the conclusion that it is highly unlikely that they are orthologs.
source: Although the DNA-binding domains of E2F/DP and SBF/MBF are both classified as wHTH proteins, they show important differences in overall structure and mode of protein-DNA complex formation that lead us to conclude that it is highly unlikely that they are orthologs.
evidence: Based on structural analysis and inference

claim: The E2F/DP family has an RRXYD DNA-recognition motif in its helix that is invariant within the E2F/DP family and is responsible for interacting with the conserved, core GCGC motif.
source: The E2F/DP family has an RRXYD DNA-recognition motif in its helix that is invariant within the E2F/DP family and is responsible for interacting with the conserved, core GCGC motif (Zheng et al., 1999) (see Figure 5A: red structure).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zheng et al., 1999 and structural data in Figure 5A

claim: The RRXYD recognition motif is strikingly conserved in E2F/DP across all eukaryotes, including the E2F/DP proteins uncovered in basal fungi.
source: The RRXYD recognition motif is strikingly conserved in E2F/DP across all eukaryotes, including the E2F/DP proteins uncovered in basal fungi (Figure 5B, left).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5B

claim: A recent crystal structure of PCG2, an SBF/MBF homolog in the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, in complex with its MCB binding site does not support the proposed mode of DNA binding via a recognition helix.
source: However, a recent crystal structure of PCG2, an SBF/MBF homolog in the rice blast fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, in complex with its MCB binding site does not support this proposed mode of DNA binding (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2015

claim: In PCG2, the wing binds to the minor groove to recognize the MCB binding site, with two glutamines in the wing (Q82, Q89) being the key elements that recognize the core MCB binding motif CGCG.
source: In striking contrast to many wHTH structures, in which the recognition helix is the mediator of DNA binding specificity, the wing of PCG2 binds to the minor groove to recognize the MCB binding site. The two glutamines in the wing (Q82, Q89) are the key elements that recognize the core MCB binding motif CGCG (Figure 5A, blue structure).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Family-specific conservation in the DNA-binding domain is observed for all members of the SBF family, including basal fungal sequences.
source: Family-specific conservation in the DNA-binding domain is observed for all members of the SBF family, including basal fungal sequences (Figure 5B, right).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The incongruences in sequence, structure, and mode of DNA-interaction between E2F/DP and SBF/MBF families strongly suggest that SBF is not derived from E2F.
source: In summary, the incongruences in sequence, structure, and mode of DNA-interaction between E2F/DP and SBF/MBF families strongly suggest that SBF is not derived from E2F.
evidence: Based on multiple lines of structural and sequence evidence

claim: The DNA-binding domain of the APSES and SBF proteins is homologous to a viral KilA-N domain.
source: Previous work has shown that the DNA-binding domain of the APSES and SBF proteins is homologous to a viral KilA-N domain (Iyer et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Iyer et al., 2002

claim: KilA-N is a member of a core set of 'viral hallmark genes' found across diverse DNA viruses that infect eubacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes.
source: KilA-N is a member of a core set of 'viral hallmark genes' found across diverse DNA viruses that infect eubacteria, archaea, and eukaryotes (Koonin et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koonin et al., 2006

claim: The wide distribution of DNA viruses and KilA-N across the three domains of life suggests that the fungal ancestor likely acquired SBF via horizontal gene transfer rather than the other way around.
source: The wide distribution of DNA viruses and KilA-N across the three domains of life suggests that the fungal ancestor likely acquired SBF via horizontal gene transfer rather than the other way around.
evidence: Based on inference from phylogenetic distribution

claim: The majority of known KilA-N domains (weighted by species, not the number of sequences) are found in prokaryotes (85%) with a smaller fraction (10%) found in eukaryotes and a smaller fraction found in DNA viruses (5%).
source: The majority of known KilA-N domains (weighted by species, not the number of sequences) are found in prokaryotes (85%) with a smaller fraction (10%) found in eukaryotes and a smaller fraction found in DNA viruses (5%).
evidence: Supported by analysis of Pfam database

claim: Within the eukaryotes, all known KilA-N domains are found in fungal genomes with three notable exceptions.
source: Within the eukaryotes, all known KilA-N domains are found in fungal genomes with three notable exceptions.
evidence: Supported by genomic survey data

claim: Trichomonas vaginalis, a parasitic excavate, has 1000+ KilA-N domains.
source: The first exception is Trichomonas vaginalis, a parasitic excavate with 1000+ KilA-N domains (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by genomic analysis shown in Figure 4F

claim: The T. vaginalis KilA-N domains have top blast hits to prokaryotic and eukaryotic DNA viruses, e.g. Mimivirus.
source: The T. vaginalis KilA-N domains have top blast hits to prokaryotic and eukaryotic DNA viruses, e.g. Mimivirus, a large double-stranded DNA virus of the Nucleo-Cytoplasmic Large DNA Viruses (Yutin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by BLAST analysis and citation

claim: The one KilA-N domain in A. pisum genome has a top blast hit to eukaryotic DNA viruses (e.g. Invertebrate Iridescent Virus 6).
source: The one KilA-N domain in A. pisum genome has a top blast hit to eukaryotic DNA viruses (e.g. Invertebrate Iridescent Virus 6).
evidence: Supported by BLAST analysis

claim: The three KilA-N domains in R. prolixus have top blast hits to prokaryotic DNA viruses (e.g. Enterobacteria phage P1).
source: The three KilA-N domains in R. prolixus have top blast hits to prokaryotic DNA viruses (e.g. Enterobacteria phage P1).
evidence: Supported by BLAST analysis

claim: The diverse and sparse distribution of KilA-N domains throughout the eukaryotic genomes is consistent with their horizontal gene transfer into hosts from eukaryotic DNA viruses and/or via engulfed bacteria that were infected with prokaryotic DNA viruses.
source: The diverse and sparse distribution of KilA-N domains throughout the eukaryotic genomes is consistent with their horizontal gene transfer into hosts from eukaryotic DNA viruses and/or via engulfed bacteria that were infected with prokaryotic DNA viruses.
evidence: Based on inference from phylogenetic distribution data

claim: The horizontal transfer of genes between Mimivirus and their eukaryotic host, or the prokaryotic parasites within the host, has been shown to be a more frequent event that previously thought.
source: In fact, the horizontal transfer of genes between Mimivirus and their eukaryotic host, or the prokaryotic parasites within the host, has been shown to be a more frequent event that previously thought (Moreira and Brochier-Armanet, 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Moreira and Brochier-Armanet, 2008

claim: There are three major phylogenetic lineages of KilA-N domains: those found in eukaryotic viruses, prokaryotic viruses, and the fungal SBF+APSES family.
source: There are three major phylogenetic lineages of KilA-N domains: those found in eukaryotic viruses, prokaryotic viruses, and the fungal SBF+APSES family.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis

claim: The fungal SBF+APSES family is monophyletic and is strongly supported by multiple phylogenetic support metrics.
source: Our results show that the fungal SBF+APSES family is monophyletic and is strongly supported by multiple phylogenetic support metrics.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: A single HGT event is the most likely scenario that established the SBF+APSES family in a fungal ancestor.
source: This suggests a single HGT event as the most likely scenario that established the SBF+APSES family in a fungal ancestor.
evidence: Based on inference from phylogenetic analysis

claim: The current phylogeny is unable to distinguish whether the SBF family arrived in a fungal ancestor through a eukaryotic virus or a phage-infected bacterium.
source: However, our current phylogeny is unable to distinguish whether the SBF family arrived in a fungal ancestor through a eukaryotic virus or a phage-infected bacterium.
evidence: Acknowledges limitation of current analysis

claim: Of all the members of the SBF+APSES family, the most likely candidate to be a 'founding' TF is SBF, as it is the only member present in all fungi.
source: Of all the members of the SBF+APSES family, the most likely candidate to be a 'founding' TF is SBF, as it is the only member present in all fungi (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on phylogenetic distribution data

claim: In budding yeast and other fungi, SBF functions in G1/S cell cycle regulation and binds a consensus site CGCGAA.
source: In budding yeast and other fungi, SBF functions in G1/S cell cycle regulation and binds a consensus site CGCGAA (Gordân et al., 2011), which overlaps with the consensus site GCGSSAAA for the E2F family (Rabinovich et al., 2008); see Figure 7A.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gordân et al., 2011 and Rabinovich et al., 2008

claim: The SBF consensus site CGCGAA overlaps with the consensus site GCGSSAAA for the E2F family.
source: In budding yeast and other fungi, SBF functions in G1/S cell cycle regulation and binds a consensus site CGCGAA (Gordân et al., 2011), which overlaps with the consensus site GCGSSAAA for the E2F family (Rabinovich et al., 2008); see Figure 7A.
evidence: Supported by citations and shown in Figure 7A

claim: The APSES regulators, Xbp1, and MBF in budding yeast bind TGCA, TCGA, ACGCGT motifs, respectively.
source: The APSES regulators, Xbp1, and MBF in budding yeast bind TGCA, TCGA, ACGCGT motifs, respectively.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of DNA binding specificities

claim: A viral origin of the SBF+APSES family—with the founding member involved in cell cycle control—suggests the hypothesis that perhaps the founder TF functioned like a DNA tumor virus protein and hijacked cell cycle control to promote proliferation.
source: A viral origin of the SBF+APSES family—with the founding member involved in cell cycle control—suggests the hypothesis that perhaps the founder TF functioned like a DNA tumor virus protein and hijacked cell cycle control to promote proliferation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from multiple lines of evidence

claim: Significant oscillations in GFP expression were observed when E2F binding sites replaced SBF sites in the CLN2 promoter, and these oscillations were coordinated with the cell cycle.
source: We observed significant oscillations in GFP expression, which were coordinated with the cell cycle.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: The amplitude of oscillations from E2F binding sites in the CLN2 promoter was dependent on the budding yeast SBF (Swi4), but not MBF (Mbp1), and disappeared when the 3 binding sites were removed.
source: Importantly, the amplitude of these oscillations was dependent on the budding yeast SBF (Swi4), but not MBF (Mbp1), and disappeared when the 3 binding sites were removed (Figure 7C–D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C-D

claim: Budding yeast SBF can bind E2F-like sites, despite the fact that Dikarya lost ancestral E2F hundreds of millions of years ago.
source: This experiment demonstrates that budding yeast SBF can bind E2F-like sites, despite the fact that Dikarya lost ancestral E2F hundreds of millions of years ago.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and phylogenetic inference

claim: E2F1 and Swi4 can bind a set of common motifs.
source: As shown in Figure 8, E2F1 and Swi4 can bind a set of common motifs.
evidence: Supported by PBM data analysis shown in Figure 8

claim: The E2F binding site variant GCGCGAAA tested in budding yeast is one of the sites commonly bound in vitro by E2F and SBF.
source: For example, the E2F binding site variant that we tested in budding yeast (GCGCGAAA, highlighted in red), is one of the sites commonly bound in vitro by E2F and SBF.
evidence: Supported by PBM data analysis

claim: There are specific motifs that can be bound only by E2F or only by SBF.
source: Most notably, the in vitro PBM data show that there are specific motifs that can be bound only by E2F or only by SBF.
evidence: Supported by PBM data analysis

claim: Differential specificity between E2F1 and SBF is mediated by the nucleotides in the 3rd and 4th positions before the invariant CG at the 5th and 6th positions.
source: The consensus E2F-only (NNSGCGSN) and SBF-only (NNCRCGNN) motifs indicate that differential specificity between E2F1 and SBF is mediated by the nucleotides in the 3rd and 4th positions (underlined) before the invariant CG at the 5th and 6th positions.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis of PBM data

claim: E2F has a strict preference for G in the 4th position, where as SBF has a strict preference for C in the 3rd position.
source: E2F has a strict preference for G in the 4th position, where as SBF has a strict preference for C in the 3rd position (Figure 8).

claim: The replacement of the ancestral positive regulation by negative regulation of asgs expression occurred via yeast that contained both systems.

claim: In the hybrid intermediate, E2F-Rb and SBF-Whi5 may have evolved to be parallel pathways whose functions overlapped to such an extent that the previously essential E2F-Rb pathway could be lost in the transition to Dikarya.

claim: Many basal fungi (e.g. Chytrids) have preserved rather than lost the hybrid intermediate.
source: Interestingly, many basal fungi (e.g. Chytrids) have preserved rather than lost this hybrid intermediate, which suggests that each pathway may have specialized functions.

claim: Chytrids exhibit both animal (e.g. centrioles, flagella, amoeboid movement) and fungal features (e.g. cell wall, hyphal growth) whose synthesis needs to be coordinated with cell division.
source: Chytrids exhibit both animal (e.g. centrioles, flagella, amoeboid movement) and fungal features (e.g. cell wall, hyphal growth) whose synthesis needs to be coordinated with cell division.

source: The origin of the hybrid network at the base of Fungi is abrupt and may have been initiated by the arrival of SBF via virus.

claim: Many tumor viruses activate cell proliferation.
source: Many tumor viruses activate cell proliferation.

claim: When SBF entered the fungal ancestor cell it might have activated the transcription of E2F target genes by directly competing for E2F binding sites with transcriptionally inactive E2F-Rb complexes.

Rather than inhibiting the inhibitor of E2F, SBF may have directly competed for E2F binding sites with transcriptionally inactive E2F-Rb complexes (Figure 9).

source: Thus, the cooption of a viral protein generated a hybrid network to ultimately facilitate dramatic evolution of the core cell cycle network in fungi.

claim: The origin of Whi5 is unclear because no homologs were found outside of fungi.
source: The origin of Whi5 is unclear because we found no homologs outside of fungi.

source: Whi5 is a mostly unstructured protein, which, like pRb, recruits transcriptional inhibitor proteins to specific sites on DNA via transcription factor binding (Huang et al., 2009; Travesa et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2009).
